Ada pressed the cheaper violin into the prize case while the teachers toasted her in the next room. The velvet caught against a splinter on its bridge. Florian stopped beside the door, his own case tucked beneath his arm.

“Taking that one on tour?”

She kept her fingers over the latch. “The award pays tuition. Nothing for the journey.”

He looked at her, then at the dining room. He had not seen the contract; she would not ask him to explain it for her. Instead she slid it across the table, leaving a place beside her for his case.

Rosin whitened the velvet lining.

# Scene bible

# State

Lio and Hana prepare one approved wedding cake, due at four; Lio's van booking ends at six. Changing the design needs a customer conversation. Soli has bought supplies, receives weekly wages from Hana's account, and was promised uninterrupted lunch. Either baker can run the shop; lifting the glaze takes both.

Lio wants the shop closed for their first date. Hana needs it open for wages. No closing time is agreed. Lio reads reluctance about the date into her refusal; Hana has mentioned only wages. The next scene precedes delivery, while the glaze cools.

# Questions

Could staggered duties protect wages, Soli's lunch, the glaze lift, and a date? This is a possibility, not an agreement. What might Lio learn by asking Hana what she meant? Their interpretations remain untested.

Working assumption: Ola and Rin can discuss the portfolio before its submission.

Ola turned the signed agreement toward Rin. “Only the blue bowl may appear in the grant portfolio.” She read the sentence without reaching for the folder beneath it. Rin's private sketch remained there, outside the permission she had just read.

On the panel, she would help evaluate Rin's former employer. Here she was supposed to help Rin. The two duties had seemed easier to separate before he sat across from her.

“Who will you be when they ask about me?” he said.

She had no answer ready. She drew the blue bowl toward the empty photography stand.

Mara opened the door and held it against the swollen sill. Water darkened the lowest shelves. Ilan knelt beside them, setting a loose board on his knees.

“Above the tide,” he said, before she asked again.

She looked toward the upper stair. Only the retired keeper had that key; Ilan's answer could not take her through the door. At noon she had called him a thief. Now the words lay between them, as stubborn as the mud beneath her shoes. Somewhere inside these walls an old vow returned after dark. She would not add another accusation to it. She crouched and steadied his board.
</prose>
The harbor bell rang twice.

<prose>
Oren lifted the ticket toward the lamp. The space for a signature stayed blank. Leda watched his mouth as if her destination might escape from it.

“I won't announce it,” he said.

He had imagined a creditor on the quay, but she had offered him no reason. Bell Quay would come first, whenever they sailed; only the captain knew the revised time. In his coat, the letter from his old love pressed against his wrist. Leda knew it existed. She knew neither its words nor the answer he might send. He folded the ticket without marking it and turned toward the captain's door.
</prose>
The rope scraped against the rail.

# Night ferry

Use [state and uncertainty](state.md) to plan the next chapter. Source: source/chapter.md. Oren and Leda have an expedition invitation; preparations are incomplete and they have not departed. Their immediate problem competes with this chance to leave.

# State and uncertainty

Oren is the ferry clerk. Leda boards with an unsigned ticket and asks him not to announce her destination. Bell Quay is the first stop before the island. Only the captain knows the revised sailing time.

Oren suspects a creditor, but Leda has not explained her motive. Treat this as his guess, not her admission. She waits at the gangway while he decides whether to call the captain; that decision remains open.

Mara braced the shelf while Ilan drove a peg into its split side. Water touched the soles of her boots. Beyond the window a mast shifted against the pale sky; somewhere out there their expedition was still being prepared.

“We could leave this for the keeper,” Ilan said.

Only the retired keeper had the upper-room key. Mara looked toward the stairs and felt her suspicion return: the ledger sold, the empty place explained. She had no proof of it. Ilan tapped the peg again.

“Hold it level.”

She lifted her end. For now, this much they could do without deciding what his hands had done before.

Oren set his pencil beside the unsigned ticket. Leda waited at the gangway, one hand closed around the rail. He had been thinking of leaving this ferry for weeks. She had noticed; neither had found words for what would follow.

“Bell Quay first,” he said.

She nodded, offering nothing else. A creditor was the explanation he had supplied himself, and he would not put it in her mouth. Only the captain knew the revised sailing time. Oren could fetch him, but the question would bring another voice between them.

He put the ticket beneath a paperweight and walked as far as the captain's door.
